source: Soloway, Ehrlich, Gold (1984) Reading a program is like reading a story (well, almost). Yale paper, Cognitive Science Society proceedings
finding: Founding definition. A programming plan is the programming version of a schema: it holds the critical information of a stereotyped action sequence. Two kinds: control flow plans (running total loop, skip guard) and variable plans (counter variable, running-total variable). Variables are told apart by role, not by syntax.
numbers: Worked example: one sentinel-controlled averaging problem (read numbers until 99999, do not count the sentinel), solved in three programs A, B, C.
quote: What makes a program plan-like rather than unplan-like is the way in which plans are composed in a program.
limits: Short paper (4 pages of text); the full TSE 1984 paper was not opened. Text is from a scan with some garbling.
agent_relevance: A plan library entry should store role, init, update and context slots, not only code text.

source: Soloway, Ehrlich, Gold (1984) Reading a program is like reading a story (well, almost). Yale paper, Cognitive Science Society proceedings
finding: Two rules of plan composition make a program unplan-like: (1) vary how typical the composed plans are, (2) bend a typical plan so it does double duty. Program A uses standard plans (read before a WHILE loop plus a count guard). Program B uses a REPEAT loop plus a skip guard (less typical). Program C reuses the counter and total initialisation to cancel the sentinel (init to -1 and -99999), the most atypical.
numbers: Three program versions A, B, C; typicality judged by the authors from Pascal textbooks and style articles.
limits: Typicality is the authors' own judgement, not measured from a corpus.
agent_relevance: Unplan-like code is code where one piece does two jobs. An agent should flag merged or double-duty steps as risk points.

source: Soloway, Ehrlich, Gold (1984) Reading a program is like reading a story (well, almost). Yale paper, Cognitive Science Society proceedings
finding: Core experiment (fill in the blank). Advanced students (end of at least second semester) got the plan-like program Alpha or the unplan-like program Beta with one line blanked, and were not told the problem. Plan-like Alpha: most people filled Count := 0 correctly. Unplan-like Beta (correct answer Count := -1): most failed, giving the typical plan answer.
numbers: Alpha: 37 correct, 10 incorrect (n=47). Beta: roughly 5 correct and 41 incorrect (n about 46); the scan of the table is garbled. Chi-square 47.7, p<0.001. Total about 93 subjects (df 91 in the time test).
limits: The table in the scanned PDF is garbled; the Beta cells are my best reading. The text also contains a likely scan error (it says more correct for Beta than Alpha, which contradicts the table and the argument).
agent_relevance: A model that fills gaps from the typical plan will make the same error on atypical code. Expect plan-completion errors when the task is slightly unusual.

source: Soloway, Ehrlich, Gold (1984) Reading a program is like reading a story (well, almost). Yale paper, Cognitive Science Society proceedings
finding: Response time confirms plan use. People took longer to read and fill in the unplan-like program, and the gap between correct and incorrect answers was larger for the unplan-like program. Simple software metrics (lines, Halstead volume, nesting) predict the opposite: Beta is shorter and flatter, yet harder.
numbers: Reading time ANOVA, plan-like vs unplan-like F(1,91)=4.60, p<0.05. Correct vs incorrect time F(1,91)=3.06, n.s. Interaction program x response significant. Mean times about 2.3 minutes (Alpha) vs about 4.0 minutes (Beta).
limits: Single experiment, advanced students only; mean times read from a garbled table.
agent_relevance: Complexity is not the same as atypicality. Difficulty for a model may track how far a task departs from stored plans, not size.

source: Soloway and Ehrlich (1984) Empirical studies of programming knowledge (IEEE Trans. Software Engineering SE-10(5), 595-609)
finding: The full founding paper claims that expert programmers hold two kinds of knowledge: programming plans and rules of programming discourse (conventions such as variable names showing function). Experts did better on plan-like programs; novices did not show the effect. Seen only as abstract and secondary descriptions; the primary text was not opened.
numbers: Design per Detienne (1990): fill-in-the-blank, plan-like vs unplan-like versions, novice vs advanced groups, an interaction of version x expertise.
limits: Not opened. Exact per-group percentages were not found in any open source this session.
agent_relevance: Rules of discourse are the part of the theory most easily lost: conventions that signal a plan's role. A scaffold could make roles explicit.

source: Detienne (1990) Expert programming knowledge: a schema-based approach (chapter in Psychology of Programming, Hoc et al. eds)
finding: Detienne's reading of Soloway and Ehrlich: experts do worse on unplan-like programs, novices are less sensitive, so version x expertise interacts. When experts failed, they gave plan-like answers (the typical value), as the schema model predicts, and did not try the odd value.
numbers: Fill-in-the-blank task, one line removed, no statement of the program's purpose. Effects: expert > novice; plan-like > unplan-like; interaction (drop larger for experts).
limits: Secondary account of the 1984 study; no cell counts given.
agent_relevance: Typicality-driven errors are the signature failure of schema use. A guardrail should force a check against the concrete case.

source: Detienne (1990) Expert programming knowledge: a schema-based approach (chapter in Psychology of Programming, Hoc et al. eds)
finding: Formal structure of a plan. A plan is a frame with slots (variables, setup, body) and slot fillers. Plans are linked two ways: specialization (a kind of) and implementation (uses). Example hierarchy: Running_Total_Loop specialized into total-controlled, counter-controlled and new-value-controlled forms; For_Loop implements the counter-controlled loop in Pascal. Plans split into strategic, tactical (language independent) and implementation (language dependent).
numbers: Counter_Variable frame: description, initialization Counter:=0, update Counter:=Counter+1, type integer, context iteration.
limits: Descriptive frame notation, not an executable model.
agent_relevance: Direct template for an agent plan library: frames with slots, two link types, and a language-independent layer above code.

source: Detienne (1990) Expert programming knowledge: a schema-based approach (chapter in Psychology of Programming, Hoc et al. eds)
finding: Program as goal and subgoal tree. A program is a tree of goals; each leaf goal is realized by a plan. Example: report-average splits into enter-data, compute-average, output-average. Rules of discourse (conventions) give the typical slot values (for example a counter named I) and so act as cues.
numbers: Worked example, no sample.
limits: Theory description only.
agent_relevance: Solved subgoals can be stored as (goal, plan, slot values) triples; this is the memory format the series calls solved subgoals.

source: Detienne (1990) Expert programming knowledge: a schema-based approach (chapter in Psychology of Programming, Hoc et al. eds)
finding: Plan activation works both ways. Detienne's think-aloud studies (programs shown one instruction at a time, Pascal) coded 269 production rules grouped into 47 general rules. Cues such as a variable named I of type integer, or initialised I:=1, evoke Counter_Variable and predict an update I:=I+1 and a loop context. Counter plus a while loop evokes a Linear_Search plan. Bottom-up (cue to schema) and top-down (schema to expected parts) both occur.
numbers: 269 rules, 47 general rules; Pascal; experienced programmers; N not stated in the chapter.
limits: N and per-rule frequencies not given. Protocols are coded by the author.
agent_relevance: Cue-to-plan retrieval plus predicted slot values is a model of how to use a library: match cues, then check each predicted slot against the code.

source: Detienne (1990) Expert programming knowledge: a schema-based approach (chapter in Psychology of Programming, Hoc et al. eds)
finding: Plans cause expectation errors. In debugging a program written by someone else, experts missed errors when they strongly expected a particular value and did not check it was present. The effect is stronger for programs the person wrote. When no cue evokes a plan (no name, no familiar structure, no documentation), experts mentally execute the code to infer its goal.
numbers: Detienne (1984) debugging experiment, as reported; N not given.
quote: the experts have difficulties to detect some errors when they strongly expect a particular value
limits: Secondary report of a 1984 conference paper.
agent_relevance: Matches guardrails G2 and G3: a recalled plan is a hypothesis, and only real output or a concrete run settles it. Self-written work carries the strongest expectations.

source: Detienne (1990) Expert programming knowledge: a schema-based approach (chapter in Psychology of Programming, Hoc et al. eds)
finding: Recall distortions show the schema at work. After debugging, experts recalled a counter named I instead of J (the lexical form was lost, the plan kept). One expert recalled while-not-V instead of repeat-until V (the prototypical slot value replaced the real one). One expert recalled a creation function that was never in the program, inserted from the stock-management problem schema.
numbers: Two experiments (Detienne 1986b), Pascal, recall after a debugging task; N not given in the chapter.
limits: Anecdotal examples of distortions; no rates given.
agent_relevance: Reconstructed memory fills gaps with the typical value. An agent that stores a solved subgoal should keep the concrete code, not only the plan label.

source: Detienne (1990) Expert programming knowledge: a schema-based approach (chapter in Psychology of Programming, Hoc et al. eds)
finding: Support and limits of the schema view. Adelson (1981): novices group program parts by surface syntax, experts by function and by procedural similarity. Rist (1986): novices mixed syntactic and plan-based chunks, experts used almost only plan-based groups, but plan use fell when programs were complex. Pennington (1987): questions on control flow were answered faster and more accurately than data flow or function, and recognition was faster within one control structure; a modification task shifted knowledge toward function and data flow; Cobol programmers were better at data flow than Fortran programmers.
numbers: Reported findings; no cell numbers given in the chapter.
limits: Chapter reports findings only qualitatively. The control-flow findings are a competing account.
agent_relevance: Plan knowledge is task and language dependent. Do not assume one fixed plan view is right for every task.

source: Detienne (1990) Expert programming knowledge: a schema-based approach (chapter in Psychology of Programming, Hoc et al. eds)
finding: Competing explanation: control flow first. Pennington (1987) found that procedural, control-flow units form the first representation and functional (plan-like) knowledge emerges later with more time or a modification goal. Widowski and Eyferth (1986): experts read usual programs in a concept-driven way and unusual ones bottom up. Detienne concludes the two views are not contradictory: schemas can also hold syntactic units, and the mix depends on language, task and reader. Role-expressive languages (Green) let experts rely on static cues; others force use of dynamic information.
numbers: Pennington Study 1: 80 professional programmers; Study 2: 40 professional programmers (from a DTIC abstract seen in a search snippet; not opened).
limits: Pennington numbers come from a search snippet of the DTIC abstract, not the paper.
agent_relevance: Plan-first reading is not universal. A scaffold should allow a control-flow trace when plans do not fit.

source: Detienne (1990) Expert programming knowledge: a schema-based approach (chapter in Psychology of Programming, Hoc et al. eds)
finding: Experts simulate to check how plans interact. Detienne and Soloway (1988): whatever the plan-likeness, experts used concrete simulation to check for unforeseen interactions, typically around a counter in an averaging loop. Littman et al. (1986): symbolic execution lets maintainers learn how functional parts interact and prevents errors when modifying one part.
numbers: Fill-in-the-blank with think-aloud; experienced programmers; N not given.
limits: Reported second-hand.
agent_relevance: Strong support for a concrete-run check at plan junctions, which is where merged-plan bugs hide.

source: Letovsky and Soloway (1986) Delocalized plans and program comprehension (IEEE Software 3(3))
finding: Plans compose in complex ways: abutted, interleaved, nested, merged. An algorithm is a composition of plans (mergesort = recursion on a binary tree + split + sort pairs + merge). A plan is a rewrite rule from a goal to subgoals in synthesis, reversible for understanding. Central claim: the chance of recognising a plan falls when its lines are spread out (delocalized) instead of close together.
numbers: Theory plus a protocol study (below).
quote: plans can be abutted, interleaved, nested, merged, and so on
limits: Claim is argued from examples, not from a quantified test.
agent_relevance: Plan composition is where errors enter. Compose plans in steps and check each junction.

source: Letovsky and Soloway (1986) Delocalized plans and program comprehension (IEEE Software 3(3))
finding: Protocol study of delocalized plans. Six professional maintainers (4 expert, 2 junior) added a restore-record feature to a 300-line Fortran 77 program (15 routines) with good documentation. Three of six finished in 90 minutes. Examples of comprehension failure came from local reading: copying NCHNGE=NCHNGE+1 into RESTORE (dirty-bit plan misread, so it writes the database too often); IREC=0 in DELETE (to block a search cache) read as record-not-found; and redundant cache variables not noticed.
numbers: N=6 (4 expert, 2 junior); 3 of 6 completed in 90 minutes; 4 of 6 visibly reacted to the line IREC=0.
limits: Six people, think-aloud, one program and one language; qualitative only.
agent_relevance: A solved subgoal stored as local text can mislead when its purpose lives elsewhere. Store the goal and where it is used, not only the lines.

source: Letovsky and Soloway (1986) Delocalized plans and program comprehension (IEEE Software 3(3))
finding: Role versus goal. Documentation gave the role of a variable (what it holds) but not its goal (why it is kept). Prescription: document the goal, and put in-line comments on non-normal updates (updates that serve a secondary goal). Non-normal updates are where delocalized plans hide.
numbers: Examples NCHNGE (goal: decide whether to rewrite the database) and IREC (non-normal update to disable a search cache).
limits: Prescription was not tested in this paper.
agent_relevance: For each stored plan, record its goal and every place it touches state. A check can flag writes to a variable that do not match its recorded role.

source: Rist (1986) Focus and learning in program design (Cognitive Science Society proceedings, Yale)
finding: Generative model of how novices build plans. Novices do not design top-down. They pick one goal, expand it locally, find new goals as they go and solve each only as far as the current context needs. The program is built up from goal solutions. Focus on the current goal creates the pieces but also many bugs when the pieces must later be combined. Top-down design with schemas appeared only late.
numbers: 7 novices (8 began, 1 dropped), beginning Pascal at Yale; 4 programs in 2 isomorphic pairs; 30 programs; about 50 hours of protocol.
quote: The program was built up from solving individual goals, not down from the problem specification.
limits: Small N; plan stages are a composite over partly overlapping subjects. Course-specific (Pascal, week 3 to 6).
agent_relevance: A local-focus failure is likely in any step-by-step agent. A final merge pass is needed where pieces meet.

source: Rist (1986) Focus and learning in program design (Cognitive Science Society proceedings, Yale)
finding: Plans develop through stages and the stage can be read from the code. Sum plan: six stages from straight rates to a retrieved schema expanded in logical order. Selection plan: five stages from separate IFs to ELSE-IF. Read plan: nine fix types for the 99999 sentinel bug, from backout (subtract 99999 and 1) to guard to double read; the double read violates the locality heuristic that one goal is done by one piece of code. Retrieved wrong plans also occurred (a taught Y/N loop-control plan was used where a sentinel was needed).
numbers: Electric bill problem (rates 9, 5, 4, 3 cents at 350, 275, 225 kwh bands). Stage counts: 6 (sum), 5 (select), 9 (read).
limits: Stage taxonomies built from 7 subjects.
agent_relevance: Expect typical repair habits (patch the value, add a guard) before the structural fix. A bug-fix operator can prefer a change of plan over a patch.

source: Robins, Rountree, Rountree (2003) Learning and teaching programming: a review and discussion (Computer Science Education 13(2))
finding: Review of the plan literature. The plan or schema is the central chunk in programming knowledge but the term varies by author (Rist: exactly what is meant by a program plan has varied considerably). Rist (1995) model: memory nodes indexed (role, goal, object) with four ports use, make, obey, control; a search cue such as (find, average, rainfall) retrieves nodes; experts retrieve and generate code in linear order, novices create plans by focal expansion backwards from the focus. The model was implemented as a program that writes Pascal from English descriptions.
numbers: Model structure: node index (role, goal, object); 4 link types; implemented generator.
limits: Review text; Rist 1995 was not opened.
agent_relevance: Closest formal model of plan memory and retrieval. Cue indexing by (role, goal, object) is an implementable library key.

source: Robins, Rountree, Rountree (2003) Learning and teaching programming: a review and discussion (Computer Science Education 13(2))
finding: Spohrer and Soloway: plan composition, not language constructs, is the main source of novice bugs. Their claim: a few bug types account for a large share of bugs; misconceptions about language constructs are less widespread than believed. Nine kinds of plan composition problem (summarisation, optimisation, previous-experience, specialisation, natural-language, interpretation, boundary, unexpected cases, cognitive load). Merged plans (one piece of code meant to do two plans) were a common source of error, often omitting a crucial subplan.
numbers: Semester-long Pascal course at Yale; 9 problem kinds. Bug catalogue per Rist: several hundred bugs from over 200 programs.
quote: many bugs arise as a result of plan composition problems
limits: Reported through a review; the CHI 1985 and HCI 1985 papers were not opened and exact bug percentages were not found.
agent_relevance: Directly relevant: if agent errors are mostly in joining correct pieces, add junction checks, not more piece-level reasoning.

source: Spohrer, Soloway, Pope (1985) A goal/plan analysis of buggy Pascal programs (Human-Computer Interaction 1(2); also Where the bugs are, CHI 85)
finding: Abstract level only. The authors explain why some novice programs are buggier than others by merged goals/plans, where several goals are met by one integrated plan. PROUST (Johnson and Soloway) reportedly finds about 75% of such bugs in novice programs for moderately complex introductory tasks (as stated in a search snippet).
numbers: 75% PROUST bug identification as reported in a snippet; not verified.
limits: Not opened; the page was blocked. The 75% figure is not confirmed from the paper text.
agent_relevance: Use as a pointer only until the full text is read.

source: Robins, Rountree, Rountree (2003) Learning and teaching programming: a review and discussion (Computer Science Education 13(2))
finding: Teaching plans. Soloway and Ehrlich (1984) explored teaching Pascal around plans; Spohrer and Soloway advise giving students a vocabulary of goals, plans, abutment and merging. Robins et al. note the open question whether schemas should be taught directly or emerge from examples and experience; support is general (skill transfer), not from a clean programming trial.
numbers: No effect sizes in the review for this point.
limits: Evidence on explicit plan teaching is thin in this review.
agent_relevance: No strong evidence that handing a plan list to a learner improves composition; test it for the agent rather than assume it.

source: Fix, Wiedenbeck, Scholtz (1993) Mental representations of programs by novices and experts (INTERCHI 93)
finding: Plan knowledge separates experts from novices only for non-trivial plans. After studying a 135-line Pascal program for 15 minutes, experts labelled complex plan segments (linear search, read-until-EOF count, sort, binary search) far better than novices, but there was no gap on elementary plans such as incrementing a counter.
numbers: 20 novices, 20 professional experts (median 7 years). Complex plan labels (out of 4): experts 3.7, novices 1.7, F(1,38)=57.58, p=.0001. Simple plan labels: experts 4.0, novices 3.7, n.s. MANOVA over 11 questions F(11,28)=8.835, p=.0001.
limits: One program, study-only task with no concrete goal (some experts found it unnatural); free-text labels scored by the authors.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: basic plans are shared by weak and strong reasoners; the gap is in recognising larger composed plans.

source: Fix, Wiedenbeck, Scholtz (1993) Mental representations of programs by novices and experts (INTERCHI 93)
finding: Experts map code to goals and track delocalized links better. Experts matched procedures to callees (6.03 vs 3.40 of 7), described procedure goals (5.2 vs 2.8 of 7) and the methods used (2.90 vs 0.85 of 4), and listed other names of the same data object across units (3.55 vs 1.43 of 7). No difference on overall program goal (6.15 vs 5.50 of 7) or on listing procedure and variable names.
limits: Alpha set to .0045 (Bonferroni over 11 tests).
agent_relevance: The expert advantage is in linking high-level goals to specific code and across scattered parts, which is what a plan library plus junction checks is meant to supply.

source: Bidlake et al. (online appendix) Summary of literature included in a systematic review of program comprehension studies
finding: Competing and later findings summarised from a systematic review. Gilmore and Green (1988): experts used plan structures as a surface level representation. Davies (1990): novices lack plan structure knowledge; intermediates have it but cannot reach it as easily as experts; only experts used discourse rules; programmers with design training used plan cues and recalled more plan structure, so plan use may come from design training, not expertise alone. Vessey (1987): programmers' knowledge structures vary a lot and are not standardised scripts; schemas are activated top-down by signposts and bottom-up when the algorithm is unfamiliar.
numbers: Study summaries only; no cell numbers in the appendix.
limits: Secondary tabular summary; primary papers not opened. Year is approximate (appendix date unknown).
agent_relevance: Plan knowledge is partly a trained skill, not just experience. A scaffold that trains plan retrieval may help on its own.

source: Bidlake et al. (online appendix) Summary of literature included in a systematic review of program comprehension studies
finding: Older recall and chunking studies that the plan theory builds on. Shneiderman (1976): experts recall ordered programs better but the gap vanishes for scrambled lines. Adelson (1981): experts chunk by function, novices by syntax. McKeithen et al. (1981): experts sort and recall reserved words by programming knowledge. Barfield (1986): experts chunk by meaningful units. Letovsky (1987): programmers move between top-down and bottom-up (opportunistic). Pennington (1987): control flow first, plan knowledge later.
numbers: Summaries only.
limits: Secondary summaries; original numbers not opened.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as chess recall: expert advantage depends on meaningful structure; for an agent, structured cues beat flat text.

source: Burkhardt, Detienne, Wiedenbeck (1997) Mental representations constructed by experts and novices in object-oriented program comprehension (Interact 97)
finding: Limits of Pennington's plan-based model. It was tested on short procedural programs. It does not handle delocalized plans in long programs, where in object-oriented code a plan spans several classes (Rist: plans and objects are orthogonal). The authors extend the model with client-server links between objects.
numbers: Model comparison only in the section read.
limits: Theory section only; empirical results of the paper not read for this use.
agent_relevance: In larger code the plan is spread over many files; the agent should keep a plan-to-location map.

source: Detienne (1995) Design strategies and knowledge in object-oriented programming: effects of experience (Human-Computer Interaction 10(2-3), 129-170)
finding: Plan retrieval versus plan creation is visible in the order of design notes. If a schema is retrieved, actions appear in execution order (top-down, forward); if not, they appear bottom-up and backward (Rist). Eight professional procedural programmers, some experienced and some new to OOP, designed a procedural and a declarative problem. The hypothesis that beginners would develop complex plans from actions and experts from objects was not supported; the procedurally driven strategy was not used significantly more by OOP beginners; method counts differed but not significantly.
numbers: N=8 professional programmers; two problems; difference in number of methods defined not significant.
limits: N=8; several predictions not supported. Plan theory was transferred to OOP and fits only in part.
agent_relevance: Order of generation is a usable signal: out-of-order or backward generation suggests no plan was retrieved.

source: Soloway, Bonar, Ehrlich (1983) Cognitive strategies and looping constructs: an empirical study (CACM 26(11)), read as a synopsis page
finding: Predecessor of the plan theory. People prefer a read-then-process loop plan (80% of written English plans). A language whose loop fits that plan (Pascal-L with loop-exit-when) gave more correct programs than standard Pascal: 52% vs 33%. Experienced Pascal programmers more often picked process-then-read, showing language shapes the stored plan.
numbers: Sentinel-averaging problem; 80% read/process in English plans; correct programs 52% (Pascal-L) vs 33% (Pascal); N not stated in the synopsis.
limits: Seen as a short synopsis, so N is missing. The same paper is opened by angle B; counted here only as a founding source.
agent_relevance: Preferred plan shape guides correct code; match the scaffold to the natural plan order.

source: Soloway (1984) A cognitively-based methodology for designing languages/environments/methodologies (ACM SIGSOFT/SIGPLAN, abstract and review)
finding: Soloway's program: observe programmers, find where they struggle, explain with knowledge structures and strategies, then design tools to fit. Expert programmers differ from novices in two things, plans and rules of discourse. Plan-like programs are much easier to comprehend than unplan-like ones because of expectations.
numbers: No new data; a methodology paper reviewed by a reader.
limits: Reviewer's abstract, not Soloway's own text.
agent_relevance: Design the scaffold around observed failure points, then test it.

source: Demirtas, Zheng, Fowler, Cunningham (2025) Generating planning feedback for open-ended programming exercises with LLMs (AIED 2025, arXiv 2504.08958)
finding: LLMs can detect classical programming plans in student code. Classifying CS1 submissions into ten plans: GPT-4o prompted reached micro-F1 0.778 (exact match 0.716); GPT-4o-mini prompted 0.672; fine-tuned GPT-4o-mini 0.782. Baselines: AST rules 0.588, CodeBERT kNN 0.550. On submissions with syntax errors the baselines fell to 0.18 and 0.46, GPT-4o stayed 0.73. Renaming variables barely changed GPT results (changes under about 0.05).
numbers: 1616 submissions; 692 passing all tests. Plan use: 77.17% of passing submissions used instructor plans vs 61.40% of those passing no tests. Wilcoxon p<.001 vs baselines.
limits: One course, ten plans, imbalanced classes (3.2% to 24.5% share). Detects plans in code; does not test composition.
agent_relevance: Models recognise stereotyped plans well and do not rely on variable names; plan labels are a workable index for a library.

source: Jiang et al. (2023) Self-planning code generation with large language models (ACM TOSEM; arXiv 2303.06689)
finding: Writing a short plan before the code helps code models, and gold plans help a lot more. On HumanEval (code-davinci-002 base): direct 48.1 Pass@1, code chain-of-thought 53.9, self-planning 60.3, ground-truth plan 74.4. Self-planning gain over direct: 25.4% on HumanEval, 11.8% on MBPP-sanitized.
numbers: HumanEval Pass@1: 48.1, 53.9, 60.3, 74.4. Pass@10: direct 75.0, chain-of-thought 68.6, self-planning 76.3, ground-truth plan 89.1.
limits: Plans are model-written steps, not a stored library of stereotyped plans. Pass@10 for chain-of-thought is below direct, so plan text can cut diversity.
agent_relevance: The gap between self-made and gold plans (60.3 vs 74.4) is the room a good plan source could fill.
